paragraphs: Chasa, a great man in Rav's time, drowned: Yevamot 121b. R. Nachman said, “By God, the fish have eaten Chasa!” Chasa's wife went and remarried, etc. Some say Rav Nachman ruled that she might remarry, because Chasa was a great man: had he emerged, the news would have become known, etc. Bava Metzia 57a, beginning: Rava said: Rav Chasa said: R. Ammi asked, etc. R. Nachman said: Rav Chasa then said: R. Ammi resolved, etc. Tosafot writes that Rav Nachman does not disagree with Chasa, his teacher, etc. I do not know the basis for Chasa's being his teacher: how could he say of his teacher, “The fish have eaten Chasa”? At least he should have said “Rav Chasa.” Ketubot 85b likewise: a man deposited an earthenware cup with Chasa; Chasa died and left no instructions. R. Nachman said, “I know Chasa was not wealthy.” He should have said “I know R. Chasa,” or at least “Rav Chasa.” It seemed likely to me that this was another Chasa, since it says “died and left no instructions”; it should have said “drowned.” But Rashi writes that this was the man who drowned in the river. This requires investigation. Rava said: Chasa—Niddah 23b. Ruth Rabbah, on “Under whose wings you have come to shelter”: R. Chasa said. I do not know the basis for Yuchasin's statement that he lived in Rav's time. Perhaps it came from Niddah 49b: Rav Chasa said, “Our great teacher”—Rashi: Rav—“said this; may the Omnipresent aid him.” But this is a scribal error: the same matter in Bekhorot 45a has R. Chisda saying, “Our great teacher said this.” Rav Chisda regularly uses this expression: Sukkah 33b, near the end, 35b. The new Talmud editions likewise read in Ba Siman, “R. Chisda said: this matter, etc.” I was pleased. Thus he lived in Rav Nachman's time.
